title: Living in Alaska | How People Live at the End of America | 4K
fullText: Somewhere below this sky, a mountain is making its own weather. Rivers of ice crack and thunder into the sea miles from the nearest road. And between the peaks, a handful of small towns hold their lights against a wilderness that outmeasures most countries. [music] This is Alaska, the largest state in America, bigger than California, Texas, and Montana put together, and home to barely 730,000 people. Here is the strange part. 82% of Alaska's communities have no road leading in or out, so people fly to the grocery store. This is also the only state that pays its residents every single year simply for living here. And hidden on one icy shore, there is a town where the entire city sleeps under a single roof. Near the end of our journey, we will also stand beside a river where giant bears wait for salmon to leap into their mouths, including one bear so beloved that the whole world voted for him. Today we cross the last frontier. From a city where moose stroll [music] past coffee stands to a tunnel that locks a whole town in for the night, chasing one [music] question. The land pulls people here, but what makes them stay? Stay with us right through to the end and you will meet a mayor with fur, a frozen city that refuses to close its [music] schools and an answer no map can show you. Our first stop is Anchorage and it does not behave like any other American city. Nearly half the people in the entire state live here in a grid of streets pressed between the cold water of Cook Inlet and the wall of the Chugach Mountains. On paper, it has everything a modern city should have. Malls, hospitals, museums, traffic reports. [music] Then a moose walks past the bus stop and the illusion of an ordinary city quietly falls apart. [music] Around 1,500 moose live inside Anchorage and in winter hundreds more drift down from the mountains when the high snow gets too deep. They sleep in front yards. They browse the hedges outside schools. Drivers here learn to read a moose's mood the way drivers elsewhere read traffic lights. Locals will tell you the rule with a shrug. The moose was here first and the moose is bigger. [music] Daily life keeps its own northern rhythm. Anchorage runs on drive-through coffee shacks, tiny wooden huts on nearly every corner, steaming in the dark of winter mornings. People order their lattes without leaving the heated cab of a pickup truck. It is a small comfort, but in a place where the December sun barely climbs above the rooftops, small comforts are taken very seriously. >> [music] >> Look toward the water and the wildness continues. Beluga whales surface in the gray tide just off [music] the coastal trail, close enough to spot from a bicycle. Overhead, cargo jets stack up in the sky. Because this remote northern city runs one of the busiest cargo airports on the planet. A crossroads [music] between America and Asia. Anchorage manages to be [music] international and untamed in the same afternoon. [music] That contrast is the first lesson of Alaska. Even in its biggest city, the wilderness is not somewhere you visit on weekends. It is a neighbor that lets itself in [music] whenever it likes. Bears wander the green belts in June, and northern lights flicker over supermarket parking lots in January. And the further we travel from these streets, the more that neighbor takes over. So we leave the coffee shacks behind and head for the places where the [music] roads themselves surrender. [music] Spread a map of Alaska across a table [music] and something remarkable appears. 82% of the communities in this [music] state are not connected to any road at all. There is no highway to them, no back route, no long way around. Alaska is not empty because it sits far away. It stays empty because the land itself, the mountains, the ice fields, the frozen ground [music] never agreed to the idea of roads in the first place. There is a reason Americans still [music] call this state the last frontier. Most of it remains exactly that, a frontier [music] wild first and settled second. [music] So Alaskans did the obvious thing. They learned [music] to fly. By most counts, roughly one in every 60 or 70 [music] Alaskans holds a pilot's license. around six times the rate in the rest of the country. Small [music] planes here touch down on gravel bars and frozen rivers and on beaches when the tide [music] pulls back far enough. A float plane in the driveway is no stranger a sight than a second car. [music] Then [music] there is the male. Since the 1970s, Alaska has run a postal program that exists nowhere else in America. It is called [music] Bypass Mail, and it flies entire pallets of groceries flour diapers [music] frozen chicken, birthday cake mix to 139 villages at the price of ordinary postage. In much of rural Alaska, the supermarket does not have a parking lot. It has a runway. Mail day in a roadless [music] village is a small festival. Families gather at the gravel airirstrip as the plane hums [music] out of the clouds and children count the boxes coming out of the hold. The pilot knows every name on his route. He carries medicine, letters from cousins [music] in Anchorage, sometimes a new pair of winter boots ordered months ago. When the weather closes in and the plane [music] cannot come, the whole village simply waits because there is no plan B with wheels on it. [music] This is what daily life [music] looks like when geography wins. And yet almost nobody out here talks about leaving. Flying stopped being [music] an adventure to them long ago. It is the school run, the grocery trip, the ambulance. A teenager out here may learn to land on a sandbar before learning to parallel park. Keep that in mind as we drive south from Anchorage toward a mountain with a hole in it and a town that solved the problem of Alaska in [music] the strangest way of all. [music] An hour south of Anchorage, the road dead [music] ends at a mountain. And in that mountain, there is a single lane tunnel shared by cars and trains. [music] It changes direction every half hour. You wait for your [music] slot, the light turns, and for 4 km, you drive through the dripping dark [music] of solid rock. Then the mountain opens and there it is. [music] Whittier, a harbor town of around 270 people, almost all of whom live in one 14story [music] building. [music] The building is [music] called Begage Towers. It went up in the 1950s for the military back when this hidden cloudcovered port was a cold war [music] secret. Today, its long corridors work [music] like streets. The grocery store is downstairs. The post office, the city offices, [music] two small churches, all of it stacked under one roof. Residents joke that you might bump into the mayor while folding your laundry. And it is not really a [music] joke. The school [music] sits next door, connected by its own small tunnel. So on the coldest [music] mornings, children walk to class in slippers without ever stepping outside. [music] About 35 students share the classrooms, and several of their teachers live a few floors above them. Homework help is never far away. As the story is told, [music] some kids knock on a teacher's door in the evening the way other kids knock to borrow a cup of sugar. And here is the detail that surprises visitors most. [music] This tiny tower at the end of America is astonishingly international. Families from Samoa, from the Philippines, from native villages along the coast, all came for the fishing industry [music] and stayed for each other. At school birthdays, the song gets sung in two or three languages before the candles go out. Isolation, it turns out, can make [music] a community wider instead of smaller. >> [music] >> Life here is not a postcard [music] and residents are the first to say so. Groceries cost [music] more because everything rides through the mountain. If your car breaks down, you feel exactly how far away the world is. And every night [music] the tunnel closes, miss it and you sleep in your car on the far side until morning. Yet, Whittier is only one of many answers Alaskans [music] have given to the same hard question. To understand the question itself, we have to go north into the cold that wrote it. Fairbanks sits near the middle of the state, far from the softening [music] breath of the ocean. And in winter, it becomes one of the coldest cities in the developed world. 40 below zero is not a catastrophe here. It is a Tuesday. Schools [music] open, mail moves, and the diner pours coffee at dawn as if nothing unusual were happening outside. [music] The record dips all the way to -66° F, set back in the 1930s, and old-timers still measure every new cold snap [music] against it. [music] The morning ritual tells you everything. People here plug in their cars the way the rest of us charge our phones. Electric cords dangle from the grill of [music] nearly every vehicle, feeding small heaters that keep engine blocks and batteries from freezing [music] solid overnight. Parking lots at schools, offices, and supermarkets come fitted with rows of public outlets waiting along the curb like tiny [music] lifelines. >> [music] >> And through all of it, the city refuses to flinch. The school district in Fairbanks does not close for cold. Not at 30 below, not at 40. The official reasoning is [music] almost tender. The buildings are warm and safe. So, the warmest place for a child on a brutal morning is inside a classroom. Businesses open, buses run. At some point, cancelling winter stopped being an option, so people simply [music] cancelled the fear of it. [music] The cold does strange, beautiful things. Exhaled breath and chimney smoke hang in the streets [music] as ice fog turning headlights into soft halos. Eyelashes [music] frost white in minutes. But we should be honest, the darkness is harder than the temperature. [music] Around the winter solstice, daylight shrinks to a few pale hours and not everyone can carry that weight. [music] Some people do leave Alaska because of these months and nobody here blames them. Then the year swings like a pendulum. By midsummer, Fairbanks floats in more than 21 hours of daylight [music] and the town spends it recklessly. Baseball games are played at midnight with no stadium lights at all. Gardens erupt with cabbages the size of armchairs. People sleep behind blackout curtains and grin about it. To live here is to lead two opposite lives in a single year and somehow to love them both. South again, the Kai River runs an impossible shade of [music] turquoise, milky and bright, colored by glacial dust ground, finer than flower. Every summer, salmon push up this water in their tens of thousands. And for Alaskan families, that run is not scenery. [music] It is the harvest. People here still fill their freezers the way farmers elsewhere fill their barns, and the whole calendar bends around it. >> [music] >> In July, entire families stand chest deep in the current with enormous dip nets. A fishery reserved for Alaska residents alone. Father's hall, kids count, grandmother's clean fish on folding tables by the tailgate. A good [music] week can put a winter's worth of red salmon in the freezer. Then come the smokeouses, small backyard [music] sheds, breathing older smoke for days, turning fish into something halfway between food and heritage. [music] Autumn adds moose to the [music] equation. One animal can mean hundreds of pounds of meat. And as many families do, the hunt ends with deliveries. A wrapped [music] package for the widow next door. Another for the elder who cannot hunt anymore. Nobody calls it charity. In the old arithmetic of the north, [music] meat shared in October comes back as help in February, and everyone remembers who [music] showed up. And then there is the strangest ritual of all, and it arrives by bank deposit. Every autumn, nearly every Alaskan, including newborn babies, receives a dividend from the state's oil savings, the permanent fund. In 2025, it came to $1,000 a person, and the [music] amount changes with the oil years. A family of five checks the account in October and finds $5,000 essentially for holding their ground. No other state on the continent does anything like it. [music] Put the freezer and the dividends side by side [music] and you can see the deal this land offers. Alaska will not make your life easy. It will make your life yours. Fish you caught meat you shared a check with your name on it for enduring the dark. Ask a canai fisherman why he stays and he will probably [music] just open the freezer and let you count. That deal was being honored on these shores long before America ever arrived, which is exactly where our road goes next. [music] >> [music] >> Down along the rain soaked southeast [music] coast, the towns of Sitka and Ketchikan keep the deepest [music] layers of Alaska's human story. The Tlingit people have lived on these shores for thousands of years, reading the tides and carving their history into cedar. Their totem poles were [music] never decoration. They are libraries, family crests, debts of honor, whole genealogies standing 30 [music] ft tall in the rain. [music] In Ketchacan, one of the world's largest gatherings of standing totem [music] poles rises out of the mist, and the carving sheds are still working. Master carvers pass the craft to apprentices [music] with adses and patience generation after generation. The town takes in around 150 in of rain a year and locals [music] call it liquid sunshine without a flicker of irony. Wooden houses perch [music] on stilts above the creek and in late summer the water beneath them boils with returning salmon. [music] Sitka wears a different layer of history. For decades, it was the capital of Russian America, a fur trading outpost called New Archangel with onion domed churches facing the Pacific. Russian bells rang over Tlingit land for more than a century until the empire, bruised and short of money after its wars in Europe, decided its farthest colony was worth more as cash. By the 1860s, the outpost had become too costly to defend and too distant to supply. The buyer was William Seard, the American Secretary of State, and in 1867, he paid $7.2 million in gold for all of Alaska. That works out to less than 2 cents an acre. The newspapers [music] howled. They called it it Seward's Folly, a frozen wasteland, a polar bear garden. On October 18th in Sitka, the Russian [music] flag came down to cannon fire and the American one went up over a purchase much of the country considered a national embarrassment. Then came gold, then fish, then timber, then oil. and Seward's folly quietly became one of the most lopsided bargains in American history. But the balance sheet misses the point that [music] Lingut already knew. The worth of this land was never only what could be taken [music] out of it. Some of it can only be stood in front of in silence, which is what the next stretch [music] of our journey is for. Start with a bay [music] that did not exist when the United States was born. 250 years ago, Glacia Bay was not a bay at all. It was a wall of ice stretching well over a 100 km. Since then, the ice has pulled back at a pace almost unheard of in the glacial world, unveiling fjords and cliffs [music] and hidden channels like a curtain being drawn very slowly off a finished sculpture. What photographs cannot carry is the sound. When a tidewater [music] glacier sheds a slab of ice the size of an apartment block, the crack rolls [music] across the water like artillery, echoing off the rock walls for miles. Kayakers say you hear this bay before you understand it. This is not a landscape that finished forming ages ago. You are watching geology happen at conversation distance. South of there, Misty Fjords earns its name every single day. Granite walls rise more than 3,000 ft straight out of narrow saltwater channels, and waterfalls thread down [music] through cloud that never quite commits to being rain. Float plane pilots cut their engines inside the fjord so [music] passengers can sit in the hush. Many say it feels less like sightseeing and more like trespassing in a cathedral. [music] And then above everything, Denali 20,310 ft, the tallest mountain in North America. Its name often translated from the Kyukon language as the tall one. The peak is so massive it bruise its own weather, wrapping itself in cloud on days that are clear everywhere else. Locals speak of visitors who came three times and never saw it. The mountain decides who gets to look. Even the road defers to it. A single ribbon of gravel runs 92 mi into Denali's [music] wilderness, and private cars are stopped at mile 15. Beyond that, the land belongs to the caribou, the wolves, and the grizzlies digging for roots on the open tundra slopes. It is a rare piece of America designed around one polite request. Leave it alone. Wonder, this state insists, comes with terms. So does winter as our next stop makes brutally clear. The road to Valdez [music] climbs over Thompson Pass and this is where Alaska stops measuring snow in inches and starts measuring it in meters. The pass averages around 550 [music] in of snowfall a year, roughly 14 m, the snowiest place in the state. In the winter of 1952, it buried itself under 974 in, [music] a season nobody here has seen match since. Down at sea level, [music] Valdez catches what the pass lets through, and that is still around 300 in [music] a year. By most counts, the snowiest town in America. Snow here is not weather. It is a second landscape that arrives every autumn and has to be managed like a rising river. Plows run in convoys. Roofs get [music] shoveled before they grown. Kids grow up doing homework beside [music] windows that slowly turn into white walls. [music] All that snow writes itself into the scenery. The mountains around town are stre with avalanche paths. And in summer, the melt turns those same lines into ribbons of waterfall. Hundreds of feet of white thread down dark rock. Heliski guides, guides, and avalanche forecasters read these slopes the way sailors read a storm because the beauty and [music] the danger are the same object seen twice. And through this white world runs an artery of black. Valdez is the final [music] stop of the Trans Alaska pipeline, an 800m steel line carrying oil from the Arctic coast [music] down to this ice-free harbor. Tankers load here all year round. It is a strange pairing, one of America's most industrial [music] ports set inside one of its most fragile looking landscapes. And the town carries both identities at once. >> [music] >> Stand on the pass at dusk and the scale settles over you. 14 m of snow every single year and still the lights of the town come on below, stubborn and golden. Nobody is stranded here against their will. They looked at the snowiest corner of the country and decided it [music] was home. Hold that thought in the silence of the pass because down river another kind of Alaskan giant [music] is waiting to meet you. [music] Across the Gulf lies Kodiak, an emerald island of fishing boats and rain. [music] and it shares its name with the largest brown bears on Earth. A grown male Kodiak bear can stand 10 ft tall and approach 1,400 lb. Fisherman and bears have lived [music] side by side here for generations, bound by an unwritten constitution. Keep your distance, [music] keep your catch clean, and never, ever surprise one another. [music] We will not pretend this is a fairy tale. Bears are dangerous neighbors and every few years somebody gets hurt. But the local answer has never been to empty the island [music] of bears. It has been caution. Bearproof bins. Loud conversation on forest trails. A thousand small habits that let two [music] apex species share one shoreline. Respect in Alaska is a survival skill and children learn to sing out on berry trails long before they memorize multiplication tables. [music] Then comes the appointment we promised you at the start. Every summer on the Brooks River in Katmmy, the salmon return with timing [music] so faithful that biologists can predict the gathering almost to the weak. The falls force the fish to leap and the big brown bears know it. The strongest males [music] claim the lip of the falls. Jaws open and the salmon fly straight into them. Younger bears wait downstream, learning the trade from 30 ft away. >> [music] >> And one of those bears became a global celebrity. His number was 480, but the world knew him as Otus, the Zen master of Brooks Falls. While his rivals brawled in the churning [music] pool beneath the falls, Otus sat apart in a calm eddy, perfectly still, and let the salmon come to him. Four times, viewers around the world crowned him champion of Fat Bear Week, the park's beloved online contest honoring the bear best prepared for winter. No other bear has ever won it four times. [music] Otus came back every summer for more than two decades. And when he finally stopped appearing, rangers believe [music] his long story had quietly ended. Though with bears, no one ever knows for certain. What he leaves behind is the lesson of this whole river. Patience outfishes fury year after year. Alaskans [music] watched him and recognized themselves. Sit through the hard season calmly enough and the river provides. One last town wants to show you how that philosophy sounds when humans live it. Torquetina waits at the end of a spur road in the shadow of Denali, a town of about 900 [music] people, log cabins and bush planes idling on skis. From here, glacia [music] pilots ferry climbers up onto the mountain itself, landing on runways of ice a mile above the valley floor. The town has one main street, a handful of old roadhouses, and a sense of humor as durable [music] as its winters. Nothing proves that humor like the town's most famous politician. For 20 [music] years, the honorary mayor of Tolkitnner, as locals happily tell it, was a golden cat named Stubs. As the story goes, a store manager named Lorie Steek found him in a box of kittens in her parking [music] lot and picked the one with no tail. From 1997 until his passing in 2017, [music] Stubs held court at the general store while 30 or 40 visitors a day arrived just to meet the mayor. The old ways still run on four legs here too. Across this region, sled dogs remain a living heritage, and towns like nearby Wasilla keep the mushing tradition close. Kennels of howling athletes, handlers who know every paw by feel. Watch a team lean into harness at 20 below, and you understand it immediately. Long before the bush [music] plane, this was how Alaska moved. And some mushers still run the old supply [music] trails for the joy of it, retracing routes their grandparents once needed. [music] Then night falls and the state pays out its final dividend. Green light unspools [music] across the sky, folding and refolding above the silhouette of Denali. The aurora at its [music] brightest here in the deep cold of the darkest months. Families pull on parkers at 2:00 in the morning and stand in the driveway, faces upturned. It is the sky's reply to a hard question. This [music] is what you get for staying. So we end where we began with the question no map can answer. What keeps [music] people here? In other places, people build good lives despite the difficulty. Alaskans chose the one state [music] where the difficulty is the point. The plugged in cars, the tunnel that locks at night, the freezer full of salmon, the check [music] that arrives for enduring the dark. Alaska is the only place in America where the land itself tests you every year, pays you for passing, and where the people who stay would not trade the test [music] for anything. If this journey across the [music] last frontier stayed with you, a like helps more travelers find their way north. And subscribing means you will [music] not miss the next country we call on. Before you go, answer us one thing below. Could you [music] make it through a full Alaskan winter? And what would get you through it? We read every [music] reply and sometimes your words decide where this channel flies next.
